label: JZ Mock B · Paper 2 · Question 1
knowledgePattern: Check which universal claims the supplied numerical fact refutes
solution:
The number 1729 meets statement 1’s hypothesis: it has the two displayed representations as sums of positive cubes. Its displayed factorisation proves it is composite, so it refutes 1.

Statement 2 assumes a prime number, whereas 1729 is composite. It therefore cannot refute 2. For 3, the same number is a product of three distinct odd primes and also one more than the cube of 12, so it refutes 3.

All the displayed prime factors of 1729 are at least 3, so this particular fact does not refute 4. A statement can be false for some other example without the supplied number being its counterexample. Thus 1 and 3 only: answer D.

hints.title: Check when each statement applies
hints.body: For each statement, write what must be true of a number before the statement makes a claim about it. Check those requirements for 1729.
hints.recap: A counterexample must first satisfy the statement’s starting conditions.
hints.pitfall: Use the fact given about 1729, not a different example.
hints.pause: Mark which statements actually apply to this number.

recall.reminder: A counterexample satisfies every assumption but fails the conclusion.

hints.title: Now test the conclusions
hints.body: For each statement that applies, compare its conclusion with the two cube sums and the prime factorisation given.
hints.recap: Only a failed conclusion makes a counterexample.
hints.pitfall: A statement can apply to a number without being disproved by it.
hints.pause: Decide which conclusions the supplied fact contradicts.

recall.reminder: An if-then statement fails when its starting condition is true and its conclusion is false.
